_readme: The roster of sites a flight fare watch may read, and what is known about each.
WHY THIS FILE IS DATA AND NOT A PYTHON TUPLE. Every other domain policy on this host is a
tuple in the script that uses it (price_search.DEFAULT_PREFER, DOMAIN_SKIP). Those encode a
PREFERENCE and change when the logic changes. This file encodes MEASUREMENTS, and it changes
when a third party redesigns a page — a different clock entirely. It is also the artifact a
human reads to answer 'why is kayak not being checked', which a tuple buried in an extractor
is not.
WHAT verdict MEANS. Nothing in here is trusted until it was measured against the live site by
scripts/flight_probe.py, twice: once on the host and once from inside a real cron tick. Until
then a site is 'untested' and flight_watch.py WILL NOT QUERY IT. That is deliberate, and it is
the whole lesson of docs/TRACKING_ENHANCEMENT.md: on 2026-08-07 a fare monitor reported
'$358.72 at high confidence' off a page whose own title said 'C$ 146+', because every guard it
had was satisfied by a number that meant nothing. A url_template written from memory is a
guess, and a guess that ships is that bug again.
untested            authored from documentation/recall, never fetched. NOT QUERIED.
usable              a fare for the requested itinerary was read from plain HTML.
usable_with_browser same, but only after JavaScript ran in headless Chromium.
blocked             the site served a robot wall, a CAPTCHA, or an empty shell to automation.
no_deeplink         a fare exists but only behind form interaction; the URL cannot carry the
itinerary. A different and much more fragile class of automation.
unusable_role       the site has no per-itinerary fare to read at all (see role).
WHY role EXISTS. The 19 sites requested are not interchangeable. Most are itinerary search
engines. Two are deal FEEDS with no origin/destination form at all — asking secretflying.com
for 'YYZ-YVR on Sep 15' is not a query it can express. Flattening that difference would build
a lie into the data, so it is a field instead.
WHY owner EXISTS. Booking Holdings owns kayak, momondo, cheapflights and priceline; Expedia
Group owns orbitz and travelocity; Fareportal owns cheapoair and onetravel. Siblings share an
anti-bot stack and a fare engine, so TWO AGREEING SIBLINGS ARE NOT INDEPENDENT CONFIRMATION,
and one sibling blocking predicts the others. flight_watch.py's quorum reads this field.
WHY currency IS NOT OPTIONAL. A '$' on orbitz.com is USD and on travelocity.ca is CAD. A USD
fare compared against a CAD target is a wrong alert that looks entirely reasonable. An unknown
currency is a hard reject, never a guess.
PLACEHOLDERS. {origin} {dest} are uppercase IATA; {origin_lc} {dest_lc} lowercase;
{depart} {ret} are YYYY-MM-DD; {depart_ymd} {ret_ymd} are YYMMDD; {adults} an integer.
A site needing anything else (kiwi.com wants city slugs) carries a code_map and is not
queried until recon fills it in.
DATE FLEXIBILITY (Phase 1e of docs/FLIGHT_WATCH_PLAN.md). When the user names a month rather
than a day, the watcher resolves it PER SITE using date_flex, which is a MEASURED capability:
whole_month  the site's own whole-month search, expressible in the URL (month_url_template).
Best evidence: the site itself is answering 'cheapest in March'.
range        accepts an explicit from-to window (range_url_template). Needs a bounded stay
length, so it is SKIPPED when trip length is unknown rather than sent unbounded.
calendar     no flex query, but a price calendar whose cells carry a price AND a date. The
`calendar` object holds the selectors for reading it.
none         neither. The watcher prices 1st-of-month out, last-of-month back, records
date_basis=assumed_month_bounds, and that reading is LOGGED BUT NEVER TEXTS
ALONE -- it is one arbitrary pair, not the cheapest in the month, and texting it
would make the reader book a worse fare believing it was the best.
unknown      not yet measured. THE DEFAULT. A month ask will not query this site.
n/a          the site takes no dates at all (a deal feed).
Placeholders for month/range templates: {depart_ym} {ret_ym} are YYYYMM, {depart_ym_dash} and
{ret_ym_dash} are YYYY-MM. Range templates additionally take {depart_from} {depart_to}
{ret_from} {ret_to} as YYYY-MM-DD.
A month-mode fare is only valid if the fare AND its own departure and return dates come out of
one itinerary element together. A whole-month results page legitimately lists dozens of
itineraries -- the same page shape that produced the $358.72 incident -- so a bare minimum with
no dates attached is rejected, and the found dates are mandatory output on every alert surface.
MEASURED 2026-08-07, plain tier, YYZ->YVR 2026-09-15/2026-09-22. Result: ZERO shippable.
blocked        10   google, skiplagged, kayak, momondo, cheapflights, priceline, trip,
orbitz, travelocity, edreams
no_deeplink     6   kiwi, cheapoair, onetravel, flighthub, airwander, flightsfinder
(never fetched — nothing learned about whether they block)
js_only         1   skyscanner (708-byte React shell: not a block, just not rendered)
unusable_role   2   secretflying, travelpricedrops (deal feeds, no O/D form)
Read the counts by OWNER, not by host, or 19 sites look like 19 chances. kayak + momondo +
cheapflights are ONE Booking backend serving one identical 'What is a bot?' wall; priceline is
a fourth Booking property refusing separately; orbitz + travelocity are ONE Expedia backend
both answering 429 on the first request ever made to them. Ten blocks are about six operators.
js_only is NOT a failure verdict. It means the page never rendered, so nothing has been learned
about whether a fare is readable — the browser tier is the test that decides.

canonical_probe._why: A dense domestic route ~5 weeks out: plenty of inventory, no seasonal edge case, and both codes are single-airport so a probe failure is never an ambiguity failure.

sites.name: Google Flights
sites.notes: PLAIN TIER 2026-08-07: HTTP 200, 512 KB, body contains 'captcha'. Served a challenge to plain urllib. It DID echo the requested dates, so the deep link is right and the itinerary reached it — only the client was rejected. Still the single best browser-tier candidate: if any site can answer, it is this one.  ||  The ?q= natural-language form is used rather than the tfs= protobuf: tfs is a base64 protobuf whose field numbering is undocumented and has changed, while q= is a documented user-facing surface. Expected to be the single most authoritative source if it can be read at all. Priced first in registry order for that reason.

sites.name: Kiwi.com
sites.code_map: REQUIRED — kiwi routes by city slug ('toronto-canada'), not IATA. Recon must record the slug derivation or this site stays untested.
sites.notes: Not fetched: no url_template could be authored, because kiwi routes by city slug ('toronto-canada') rather than IATA and the derivation is unverified. Nothing was learned about whether it blocks. Chrome recon should capture the slug form and its JSON endpoint before this is retried.  ||  Worth probing early despite the slug problem: kiwi's own frontend calls a documented-shaped GraphQL/umbrella endpoint, and a JSON endpoint beats DOM scraping on every axis — stability, size, and not needing a browser at all. Recon target #1 for the network tab.

sites.name: Skiplagged
sites.notes: PLAIN TIER 2026-08-07: HTTP 403, 5.6 KB, 'enable javascript and cookies'. Hidden-city caveat stands regardless, so even a successful read would ship with a warning.  ||  Its frontend calls an internal JSON search endpoint — recon should capture it. HIDDEN-CITY CAVEAT IS LOAD-BEARING: skiplagged's cheapest results are throwaway-ticket itineraries that forbid checked bags and breach airline terms. If this site ever supplies a winning fare, the alert must say so, because a fare the user cannot actually use as booked is the same class of wrong as a teaser.

sites.name: Kayak
sites.notes: PLAIN TIER 2026-08-07: HTTP 200 but 305 KB titled 'What is a bot?'. An anti-bot wall dressed as a page — no fare-shaped number and neither date echoed. IDENTICAL wall to momondo.ca and cheapflights.ca: one Booking Holdings backend, three hosts, one measurement.  ||  URL grammar is stable and well known. Expectation before measuring: among the most headless-hostile sites on the web, and its results stream in progressively so a fare read too early is a partial-result fare. Note currency is USD on the .com — the user named kayak.com specifically.

sites.name: Momondo
sites.notes: PLAIN TIER 2026-08-07: HTTP 200, 267 KB, titled 'What is a bot?'. Same wall as kayak.com and cheapflights.ca — the owner field predicted this exactly.  ||  Kayak's sibling on the same engine. If kayak.com blocks, expect this to block identically — and if BOTH return a fare, the owner field means they count once, not twice.

sites.name: Cheapflights
sites.notes: PLAIN TIER 2026-08-07: HTTP 200, 252 KB, titled 'What is a bot?'. Worth recording precisely because this is the site that produced the $358.72 incident: the 97-price route page that fabricated a fare is now behind a bot wall, so the old failure is no longer even reachable by this path.  ||  THIS IS THE SITE THAT CAUSED THE REFUSAL. On 2026-08-07 its route page served a JSON-LD offers array holding 358.72, 360.12, 362.92, 364.32 and more — 97 distinct prices, a list of unrelated itineraries — and price_search reported the first one as a $358.72 fare at high confidence. price_watch.py:129 LISTING_MIN_PRICES was measured on this exact page. Any fare read here must survive itinerary binding, not just be a number on the page.

sites.name: Priceline
sites.notes: PLAIN TIER 2026-08-07: HTTP 403, 5.4 KB, 'access to this page has been denied'. Fourth Booking Holdings property, fourth refusal.  ||  The dated-leg URL grammar takes YYYYMMDD without separators in some versions and ISO in others; recon must pin which. Fourth Booking-Holdings property in this roster — the owner field is doing real work here.

sites.name: Skyscanner
sites.month_note: The YYYYMM date segment is a long-standing documented Skyscanner URL form ('/202603/202603/' = any March, both ways). Written from recall, NOT measured: verdict stays untested and the watcher will not use it until flight_probe.py confirms the page returns fares carrying their own dates.
sites.notes: BROWSER TIER 2026-08-07: HTTP 200, 8240 bytes, body carries 'captcha', 'px-captcha' and 'human verification' — PerimeterX. This CLOSES the roster's last open question. The plain tier's 708-byte React shell was not a site that merely needed rendering: rendering it produces a PerimeterX challenge instead of a page. js_only -> blocked.  ||  PLAIN TIER 2026-08-07: HTTP 200 and only 708 BYTES — a bare React shell ('<div id="root">' plus 'You need to enable JavaScript to run this app'). NOT a block and NOT an empty site: the page simply has not rendered. THE ONE GENUINE BROWSER-TIER CANDIDATE in the roster, and the only site whose month_url_template is already authored.  ||  Lowercase IATA and YYMMDD dates — the only site in the roster using the short date form, which is why {origin_lc}/{depart_ymd} placeholders exist at all. Expectation before measuring: aggressive bot detection, on a par with kayak.

sites.name: Trip.com
sites.notes: PLAIN TIER 2026-08-07: HTTP 432 with a 17-byte body reading 'whaleguard block' — Trip.com's WAF, refusing before any page exists. 432 is non-standard, which is why a hand-listed status check missed it.  ||  Takes currency and locale as explicit query parameters, which is unusually cooperative and makes the currency field verifiable rather than assumed. Its frontend calls a JSON search endpoint worth capturing.

sites.name: Orbitz
sites.notes: PLAIN TIER 2026-08-07: HTTP 429, 244 KB. Rate-limited on the FIRST request this host ever made to it, so it is fingerprinting rather than throttling. Same Expedia backend as travelocity.ca, same result.  ||  Expedia Group's shared Flights-Search grammar; the TANYT suffix means 'any time of day'. Sibling of travelocity.ca below — same engine, same expected blocking behaviour, counts once in a quorum.

sites.name: Travelocity
sites.notes: PLAIN TIER 2026-08-07: HTTP 429, 243 KB. Identical to orbitz.com — one Expedia backend, two hosts.  ||  Same grammar as orbitz.com but a Canadian storefront, so CAD. If exactly one Expedia property survives recon, prefer this one: a CAD fare needs no conversion to compare against a CAD target.

sites.name: eDreams
sites.notes: PLAIN TIER 2026-08-07: HTTP 403, 8.4 KB. Note its itinerary lives in a URL hash fragment, which is never sent to the server, so the plain tier could never have worked here even without the 403.  ||  The itinerary lives in a HASH FRAGMENT, which is never sent to the server — so this URL cannot work without a browser under any circumstances, and a plain-urllib tier-1 probe of it is guaranteed to be meaningless. Skip tier 1 for this site.

sites.name: CheapOair
sites.notes: Not fetched: no slot-bearing URL could be authored (Fareportal's listing URL carries an encoded search token). Nothing learned about blocking.  ||  No deep-link grammar authored: Fareportal's listing URL carries an encoded search token rather than plain slots, so a template written from recall would be a fabrication. Recon must either capture a slot-bearing URL or set verdict=no_deeplink. Sibling of onetravel.com.

sites.name: OneTravel
sites.notes: Not fetched: same Fareportal engine as cheapoair.ca, same missing deep link.  ||  Fareportal's other storefront, same engine as cheapoair.ca. If one gets a deep link the other almost certainly takes the same grammar with a different host — but they still count as ONE source in a quorum.

sites.name: FlightHub
sites.notes: Not fetched: results believed to sit behind a POSTed search returning a session-scoped URL. Unmeasured, so recorded as unknown rather than blocked.  ||  Canadian OTA. Results are believed to live behind a POSTed search that returns a session-scoped URL, i.e. no_deeplink — but that is an expectation, not a measurement, so it is recorded here rather than acted on. Recon decides.

sites.name: AirWander
sites.notes: Not fetched: no URL grammar authored. Multi-stop specialist, so a plain round trip may not be its question even if it can be reached.  ||  A multi-stop / stopover specialist, not a plain A-to-B engine: its whole product is inserting a stopover city. For a simple round trip it may return nothing useful even when it works perfectly. Small site, so likely the least defended in the roster — worth probing precisely because the well-known ones are expected to block.

sites.name: FlightsFinder
sites.notes: Not fetched: no URL grammar authored. Small metasearch, plausibly the least defended host in the roster — worth Chrome recon before writing it off.  ||  Small UK metasearch. Same reasoning as airwander: low traffic often means low defences. May prove to be redirect_only — a referral shell that shows a teaser and hands off to an OTA for the real price.

sites.name: Secret Flying
sites.notes: Not applicable by role: a deal feed with no origin/destination form. It cannot express 'YYZ-YVR on Sep 15' at any tier. Its RSS remains useful as a SECONDARY route-match signal, never as a fare source.  ||  AN ERROR-FARE AND DEAL FEED, NOT A SEARCH ENGINE. It cannot answer 'YYZ to YVR on Sep 15' — there is no form to ask. Included because the user named it and because it is genuinely useful in a different way: a cheap RSS poll can spot a published deal that MATCHES a watched route, with no browser and no bot risk. It supplies a SECONDARY signal ('a deal was posted for your route'), never the fare a threshold is compared against, because the posted price is a third party's claim about a fare at an unknown time — the same reason web_search.snippet_prior refuses to let a snippet number become a price.

sites.name: Travel Price Drops
sites.notes: Not applicable by role, as secretflying.com. Whether it publishes RSS at all is still unverified.  ||  Same class as secretflying.com: a deal feed with no origin/destination query. feed_url is null because whether it publishes RSS at all is unverified — recon confirms or sets unusable_role. Secondary signal only, on the same reasoning.
